Angina and a heart attack are two different conditions affecting the heart. 

Angina is a type of chest pain that occurs when the heart does not receive enough oxygen-rich blood. It is often described as a squeezing or pressure sensation in the chest, and may also be felt in the arms, neck, jaw, shoulder, or back. It typically occurs during physical activity or emotional stress, and is relieved with rest or medication such as nitroglycerin. Angina is often a symptom of coronary artery disease, where the arteries that supply blood to the heart become narrowed or blocked. 

A heart attack, on the other hand, occurs when blood flow to the heart is completely blocked, usually by a blood clot. The lack of oxygen causes damage to the heart muscle, which can be life-threatening if not treated promptly. Symptoms of a heart attack include severe chest pain or pressure that may radiate to the arms, jaw, or back, shortness of breath, sweating, nausea, or lightheadedness. 

Diagnosis of angina and a heart attack may involve a physical exam, medical history, and various tests such as an electrocardiogram (ECG), stress test, cardiac catheterization, or imaging tests such as an echocardiogram. 

Treatment for angina may involve lifestyle changes such as quitting smoking, exercising regularly, and following a heart-healthy diet. Medications may also be prescribed to help manage symptoms and prevent further heart damage, such as nitroglycerin, beta-blockers, calcium channel blockers, or aspirin. In some cases, procedures such as angioplasty or bypass surgery may be necessary to improve blood flow to the heart. 

For a heart attack, emergency treatment is critical and may involve medication to dissolve the blood clot, procedures such as angioplasty or stent insertion to reopen blocked arteries, or in some cases, bypass surgery.
